title: ticket-and-task
intention: Every workflow instance is flagged, at /intent, as a TICKET or a TASK. A ticket's intention joins the FABRIC — the set of records that say what the system IS — at cast, before any work is done. A task is work the system needs done that does not define it. Both are workflows: same machinery, same mutable string, different relationship to the fabric.
why:
Akien, 2026-07-22, from 'yank the UU debris out of ~/bin': 'that right there is work that doesn't result in code, has an intention, but that intention is really complete when it's done.' Until now every ticket answered the same way — FREEZE into the component's history as provenance — so the question never had to be asked. The debris yank is the first member that answers differently, and it exposed that the disposition was never actually decided, only defaulted.

The distinction earns its cost by DERIVING what used to be chosen. Because a ticket moves the definition at cast, its voyage MUST freeze beside the code — the fabric changed, so provenance is owed (Law 5). Because a task can be cast, run, and completed with the definition never moving, there is no component whose charter its story is provenance OF — so depot-and-forget is not a policy call, it is what remains. One flag, two dispositions, no judgment at resolve time.
traces_to: Law 1 (the resolver is spent on the novel) — the flag is the seed test, which is Law 1 stated as a partition question: would a co-developer, lacking this, re-derive something we already settled?
Law 5 (intent, its voyage, and its proofs share an address) — the flag decides WHETHER an address is owed at all; a task has no component to sit beside.

Law 7 (records of truth are permanent) — a ticket's history is a record of truth and freezes; a task's is a receipt and may expire. The flag is what distinguishes them, so without it Law 7 has no way to know which it is looking at.

falsifier.proves_green: quorum signature gate — N human readers read and restate it back; recorded as a VALIDATION with method = 'review by N readers', caller = the reviewers, evidence = their restatement. Verdict (reviewers) and seal (notary) are different hands here; do not collapse them.
falsifier.proves_red:
The distinction is WRONG if the seed test is soft — if, across the first ten nodes cast through the flagged /intent, two readers place any node differently. A test that needs adjudication is not a test, and this one has to be answerable from the WHAT alone or it does not belong at /intent.

It is INCOMPLETE if the empty cell fills: TRANSIENT BUT SHAREABLE — a one-shot every Cairn user needs (a corrective for a bad release, say). Judged genuinely empty today, because the migrations we have (charter -> state+history) change the fabric and are therefore tickets. A real member is the signal to revisit, not a reason to pre-build.

Wrong-INTENT signal (the one to watch hardest): if TASK becomes the cheap escape hatch and the fabric quietly stops recording itself, the flag has become a loophole and is doing the opposite of its job — the UU disease in a new costume.
falsifier.horizon: The first ten nodes cast through a flagged /intent. Measure: disagreement rate on the flag (target zero), and the ticket:task ratio (a collapse toward task is the wrong-intent signal firing).

how:
Add ticket/task flag at /intent. A ticket's intention joins the fabric (what the system IS); a task is perishable work (yank debris, rename files). The flag determines which records persist and which age out.

OPERATIONAL SHAPE (Akien, 2026-09-04): most tasks are either AD-HOC ('remove all the files in ~ that end in .dontneed' — one-shot, typed by a human, not recurring) or MACHINE-GENERATED (a probe fires, a trouble ticket opens, a watch sees something that needs doing). When an ad-hoc task recurs, the recurrence is the signal to write a development ticket that automates it — the task PROTOTYPES the ticket. Most tickets are development tickets. Most tasks are LIKELY to be automatically generated.

THE QUESTION LIVES AT /SORTED (or earlier, at cast or even /intent): 'is this a task?' The answer is in the WHAT — does this change what the system IS, or just do something the system needs done? No separate /task skill needed; it is one field in the cast. The flag could also surface in the operator inbox or dashboard as a filter (tasks vs tickets).
